title: Hazard Awareness & Anticipation
whatItIs: Scan near and far, read the clues, predict what others will do and act early, so you never have to react at the last moment.
keyFacts: The national standard: scan near and far, use visual clues to predict hazards, then judge and prioritise them.
Drive at a speed that lets you stop safely within the distance you can see to be clear.
In side roads and country lanes, look out for unmarked junctions where nobody has priority.
Pedestrians, especially children, who are looking the other way may step out without seeing you.
Residential streets: expect car doors opening, vehicles moving off and children between parked cars.
ADI hazard perception: 14 clips, up to 5 points per developing hazard, pass mark 57 out of 75.

visual.caption: Clues that a hazard may be developing

items.title: Parked car, indicator starts to flash
items.text: Now it's moving off and you'd need to slow down: it has become a developing hazard.

items.title: Bus stops and ice cream vans
items.text: People may emerge suddenly; children may run into the road. Drive carefully and slowly.

items.title: A rider looks over their shoulder
items.text: They may be about to pull out, turn right or change direction: give them time and space.

items.title: A large vehicle ahead
items.text: It may need extra room to turn, or be dealing with a hazard you cannot see: hang back.

a.label: Not a developing hazard
points: A parked car at the roadside that is doing nothing
It wouldn't make you change speed or direction

b.label: Developing hazard
points: Something that would make you act: change speed or direction
Click as soon as it starts to develop to score highly

onTheTest.question: In the ADI hazard perception test, what makes something a 'developing hazard'?
options: It is visible anywhere in the clip
It would cause you to take action, like changing speed or direction
It involves a pedestrian or cyclist
It appears in the last 10 seconds of the clip
onTheTest.why: GOV.UK ADI part 1: a developing hazard is something that would cause you to take action, like changing speed or direction. You score up to 5 points for each one.

onTheTest.question: On test, a candidate notices a cyclist late and reacts suddenly at the last minute, compromising the cyclist's safety. How does DT1 mark this?
onTheTest.why: DT1 11.11 Awareness/planning: a late reaction to other road users is a driving fault; a last-minute, sudden reaction that compromises their safety is a serious fault.

traps: In the hazard perception test, clicking continuously or in a pattern scores nothing for that clip.
Eco-safe 'planning' (hazard awareness, anticipation) is recorded on the driving test but doesn't affect the result.
Driver aids don't replace looking: act on what is in front of you, not just the sat nav or sensors.
A vehicle signalling may not turn: an indicator may not have been cancelled.
